prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)  -- The Taliban in Afghanistan have momentum that makes any effort to negotiate with them difficult, the U.S. defense secretary said. Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday. He's visiting Afghanistan on Wednesday. Secretary Robert Gates spoke to CNN's Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before leaving for Afghanistan, where he is visiting troops and bases Wednesday. "The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point," Gates said in the interview. "They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult." As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and Afghanistan government are attempting to reach out to elements of the Taliban who are engaged in the battle for financial gain, rather than ideological gain. "There are really two groups we're talking about -- the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed. The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we'll probably have to wait awhile before there's an opportunity there." On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson interviewed a spokesman for the Taliban, Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban will only negotiate with the Afghanistan government when the United States leaves the country. "Our conditions are clear, we want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country," Mujahid told CNN. Gates said the stance was not surprising. "Well I don't know what else he'd say. He's leading the opposition, he's leading this insurgency. He's not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say 'We're ready to negotiate, we're about done here,' " Gates said. The United States is adding 21,000 troops to the Afghanistan battlefield. The majority will be moving to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border. The Taliban have had mostly free rein in that area with few U.S. or coalition forces to confront them until now. Gates admitted moving the battle to the south will mean there is "a tough fight ahead." "I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we're clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched," he said. "And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties." In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has seen the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that the increased fighting in southern Afghanistan will only push the Taliban back to the Pakistani side. "Well I think it's just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy," Gates said. Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperation efforts between the two countries to deal with the problem, and by Pakistan's recent confrontation with the Taliban in Bunir province, near the capital of Islamabad. "The signs right now are pretty positive," he told CNN.

outputs.L1:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN) — The Taliban’s momentum in Afghanistan is making efforts to negotiate with the group difficult, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said.

Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and spoke with CNN’s Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before departing for Afghanistan, where he was scheduled to visit troops and military bases Wednesday.

“The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point,” Gates said. “They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult.”

As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and the Afghan government are attempting to reach out to Taliban elements motivated by financial rather than ideological considerations.

“There are really two groups we're talking about — the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed. The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we'll probably have to wait awhile before there's an opportunity there.”

On Monday, CNN’s Nic Robertson interviewed Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the group would negotiate with the Afghan government only after the United States leaves the country.

“Our conditions are clear, we want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country,” Mujahid told CNN.

Gates said the position was not surprising.

“Well I don't know what else he'd say. He's leading the opposition, he's leading this insurgency. He's not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say, ‘We're ready to negotiate, we're about done here,’” Gates said.

The United States is deploying an additional 21,000 troops to Afghanistan. Most will be sent to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous border with Pakistan. Until now, the Taliban have operated with largely free rein in the area, facing few U.S. or coalition forces.

Gates acknowledged that shifting the battle southward would mean “a tough fight ahead.”

“I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we're clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched,” he said. “And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties.”

In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has watched the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that intensified fighting in southern Afghanistan will merely push the Taliban back into Pakistan.

“Well I think it's just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy,” Gates said.

Gates said he was encouraged by recent cooperation between the two countries in addressing the problem, as well as by Pakistan’s recent confrontation with the Taliban in Buner province, near the capital, Islamabad.

“The signs right now are pretty positive,” he told CNN.

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN) —** The Taliban’s growing strength in Afghanistan is making negotiations increasingly challenging, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said.

Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday and was scheduled to travel to Afghanistan on Wednesday. In an exclusive interview with CNN’s Chris Lawrence on Tuesday evening, before departing, Gates discussed his planned visits to U.S. troops and military bases.

According to Gates, the Taliban’s political leadership is unlikely to be considering compromise or reconciliation at present because it believes it is gaining ground.

“They probably feel like they have the momentum with them,” he said, adding that meaningful talks would remain difficult unless that perception changed.

One element of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan involves efforts by the American military and the Afghan government to approach Taliban members who fight primarily for money rather than because of deeply held ideological beliefs.

Gates said these fighters broadly fall into two categories: younger or less committed members who participate mainly to support themselves and feed their families, and others driven by stronger ideological convictions. He said persuading the second group would be much more difficult and that opportunities to engage them might not emerge for some time.

On Monday, CNN’s Nic Robertson interviewed Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the organization would enter talks with the Afghan government only after the United States withdrew from Afghanistan and stopped intervening in the country’s internal affairs.

“Our conditions are clear,” Mujahid told CNN. “We want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country.”

Gates said that position was predictable. As a leader of the insurgency and opposition, he said, Mujahid could hardly be expected to announce that the Taliban was nearly finished and ready to negotiate.

The United States is deploying an additional 21,000 troops to Afghanistan. Most will be sent south to challenge Taliban forces operating near the loosely controlled border with Pakistan. Until now, the Taliban have largely operated without significant resistance in that region because relatively few U.S. or coalition troops have been stationed there.

Gates acknowledged that expanding operations into southern Afghanistan would bring difficult fighting. He said U.S. and coalition forces would be entering places where neither they nor Afghan troops had previously maintained a presence and where the Taliban were firmly established.

He also warned that increased military activity and operations would probably result in more casualties.

In recent weeks, Taliban forces have gained control of territory on Pakistan’s side of the Afghan-Pakistani border. Pakistani officials have privately told the United States they fear intensified combat in southern Afghanistan could simply drive Taliban fighters back across the frontier into Pakistan.

Gates said extremists are present on both sides of the border and pose a danger to the elected governments of Afghanistan and Pakistan. As a result, he said, the two countries share a common enemy whether they welcome that reality or not.

He added that he was encouraged by recent cooperation between Afghanistan and Pakistan in addressing the threat. Gates also pointed positively to Pakistan’s recent military action against the Taliban in Bunir province, near Islamabad.

“The signs right now are pretty positive,” Gates told CNN.

Despite these challenges, the U.S. and Afghan governments are seeking to reach Taliban fighters who may have joined the insurgency primarily because of financial hardship rather than a strong ideological commitment.

Gates suggested that these less-committed fighters could be more easily persuaded to abandon the insurgency and reintegrate into Afghan society. By contrast, he said that reconciling with ideologically committed Taliban members would be far more difficult.

Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid, however, said the group would negotiate with the Afghan government only if the United States ended its interference and withdrew from Afghanistan. His statement underscored the significant obstacles facing reconciliation efforts.

Meanwhile, the United States is reinforcing its military presence in Afghanistan by deploying an additional 21,000 troops to the conflict.
outputs.L4:
U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said negotiations with the Taliban would remain difficult as long as the insurgency believed it had momentum on the battlefield. Taliban leaders who thought they were succeeding militarily would have little incentive to compromise or enter serious talks, he argued.

The U.S.-Afghan strategy therefore combined political outreach with increased military pressure. Afghan authorities would seek to reconcile with insurgents who had joined the conflict for money, security, or other practical reasons rather than from a deep commitment to the Taliban’s ideology. At the same time, the United States planned to deploy 21,000 additional troops to strengthen security and challenge the insurgency.

Gates suggested that less committed fighters might be persuaded to abandon the Taliban relatively quickly if they were offered credible alternatives and a path back into their communities. Reaching senior Taliban leaders, however, would be far more difficult. Those driven by ideology were unlikely to negotiate while they believed the war was moving in their favor.

For that reason, Gates said military and political efforts had to reinforce each other. Additional troops and stronger Afghan security forces were intended not only to improve conditions on the ground but also to change the insurgents’ calculations. Only when the Taliban’s momentum had been slowed or reversed, he concluded, would its leaders face meaningful pressure to consider reconciliation and negotiations.

# Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: A Capital of Heritage and Ambition

Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia, is a dynamic city where deep-rooted traditions meet rapid modernization. Located in the heart of the Arabian Peninsula, Riyadh serves as the Kingdom’s political, financial, and administrative center. Once a small desert settlement, it has grown into one of the Middle East’s largest and most influential cities.

The city’s heritage can be explored at landmarks such as Al Masmak Palace and the historic district of Diriyah, a UNESCO World Heritage Site closely connected to the origins of the Saudi state. Traditional markets, including Souq Al Zal, offer visitors a glimpse of local craftsmanship, antiques, spices, and Arabian culture.

Modern Riyadh is equally impressive. Its skyline features striking buildings such as the Kingdom Centre and Al Faisaliah Tower, while new business districts, transport networks, entertainment venues, and cultural attractions continue to transform the city. This development reflects Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, which aims to diversify the national economy and expand tourism, technology, culture, and leisure.

Riyadh also provides a rich culinary experience, ranging from traditional Saudi dishes such as kabsa and jareesh to international fine dining. Major festivals, sporting events, exhibitions, and concerts attract visitors from across Saudi Arabia and around the world.

With its combination of history, hospitality, and ambitious growth, Riyadh offers a fascinating introduction to modern Saudi Arabia. It is a city that honors its past while confidently building its future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Defense Secretary Robert Gates saying the Taliban’s momentum makes negotiations difficult, incorporating his interview with Chris Lawrence and the planned U.S. troop increase in Afghanistan.
counterfactuals.output:
# Gates: Taliban momentum complicates Afghan negotiations

**WASHINGTON** — The Taliban’s battlefield momentum must be halted before meaningful negotiations can take place in Afghanistan, Defense Secretary Robert Gates said in an interview with CNN’s Chris Lawrence.

Gates said insurgents are unlikely to pursue reconciliation while they believe they are gaining ground against U.S., NATO and Afghan forces. Any serious effort to bring Taliban members into the political process, he said, depends on first reversing that perception.

“The Taliban have the momentum right now,” Gates told Lawrence, adding that prospects for significant reconciliation would improve only after that momentum is stopped and reversed.

His comments come as the United States prepares to send about 30,000 additional troops to Afghanistan under President Barack Obama’s revised war strategy. The buildup is intended to strengthen security in population centers, disrupt Taliban networks and give Afghan forces more time and support to assume responsibility for the country’s defense.

The deployment will bring the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan to nearly 100,000 troops, alongside forces from NATO allies and other coalition partners.

Administration officials have emphasized that reconciliation does not necessarily mean negotiating with the Taliban’s most committed leaders. Instead, the strategy seeks to persuade lower-level fighters to abandon the insurgency, provided they renounce violence, sever ties with al Qaeda and accept Afghanistan’s constitutional system.

Gates cautioned, however, that such efforts will remain difficult as long as Taliban commanders and fighters believe they can outlast coalition forces.

The troop increase is designed in part to change that calculation by putting sustained pressure on insurgents while improving security for Afghan civilians. U.S. officials also hope the buildup will create conditions for a gradual transfer of responsibility to Afghan security forces.

Obama has said U.S. forces could begin withdrawing in July 2011, though officials have stressed that the pace would depend on conditions on the ground. Gates’ remarks underscore the administration’s immediate challenge: weakening the Taliban enough to make reconciliation appear more attractive than continued fighting.

## Gates says military pressure is key to Taliban reconciliation as coalition losses rise

**WASHINGTON —** Former U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said prospects for meaningful reconciliation with the Taliban would depend on sustained military pressure, warning that insurgent leaders were unlikely to negotiate seriously while they believed they could prevail on the battlefield.

Gates’s comments came amid mounting casualties among U.S. and allied forces in Afghanistan and continuing concern over insurgents’ ability to operate across the mountainous border with Pakistan.

While supporting Afghan-led efforts to persuade rank-and-file fighters to abandon the insurgency, Gates drew a distinction between reintegration of local combatants and a broader political settlement with senior Taliban leaders. Any talks with the movement’s leadership, he said, would have to take place from a position of strength and require insurgents to sever ties with al Qaeda, renounce violence and accept Afghanistan’s constitutional order.

The immediate objective of coalition operations was therefore to reverse the Taliban’s momentum and convince its commanders that they could not achieve victory by force. Gates cautioned that such a shift would take time and that a major political breakthrough should not be expected before the military balance had changed.

His assessment underscored the tension at the heart of the coalition strategy: intensifying combat in order to create conditions for an eventual negotiated settlement. The deployment of additional U.S. troops and expanded operations in Taliban strongholds had produced heavier fighting, contributing to a rise in coalition deaths.

Gates acknowledged that casualties could remain high as more forces moved into contested areas and sought to protect population centers, disrupt insurgent networks and expand Afghan government control. Officials have argued that increased losses do not necessarily indicate that the strategy is failing, because troops are operating in places where coalition forces previously had little or no presence.

Nevertheless, the growing death toll has placed additional political pressure on governments contributing troops to the NATO-led mission. Public support for the war has weakened in several allied countries, while commanders have faced demands to demonstrate progress in building Afghan security forces and transferring responsibility to Kabul.

Security along the Afghanistan-Pakistan frontier remained another central challenge. Taliban and allied militant groups have long used remote border districts as transit routes and, according to Western officials, as areas for planning, training and resupply. The rugged terrain, limited government presence and difficulty of coordinating operations on both sides have allowed fighters to move through parts of the region despite military pressure.

Gates said cooperation with Pakistan was essential to reducing the threat. Pakistani forces had undertaken operations against militants in several tribal areas, but U.S. officials continued to press Islamabad to act against networks that focused their attacks on Afghanistan.

At the same time, Gates stressed that the border could not be completely sealed. Improving security would require closer intelligence sharing, better coordination between Afghan, Pakistani and coalition forces, and stronger government authority in communities on both sides.

The defense secretary’s remarks reflected the broader U.S. view that military action alone could not end the war. Washington has backed reconciliation under Afghan leadership, but has insisted that any settlement must prevent Afghanistan from again becoming a sanctuary for al Qaeda or other international terrorist groups.

For the coalition, the central question is whether battlefield pressure, stronger Afghan institutions and improved regional cooperation can weaken the insurgency enough to make negotiations credible. Gates made clear that reconciliation remained part of the eventual political solution, but said it would become realistic only when Taliban leaders concluded that continued fighting offered no path to victory.

# Gates: Taliban Not Yet Ready for Talks as U.S. Sends 21,000 More Troops to Afghanistan

**WASHINGTON —** Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Taliban is not yet prepared for serious negotiations, warning that insurgent leaders still believe they can prevail militarily as the United States deploys 21,000 additional troops to Afghanistan and prepares for intensified fighting in the country’s south.

Gates said political reconciliation remains essential to ending the war, but meaningful talks are unlikely until U.S., NATO and Afghan forces reverse the insurgency’s momentum.

“The Taliban have to feel that they are under military pressure and are not winning before they will be willing to negotiate seriously,” Gates said, outlining an approach that combines combat operations with efforts to draw lower-level fighters away from the insurgency.

American officials distinguish between hard-line Taliban leaders closely aligned with al-Qaeda and fighters motivated by money, tribal rivalries, local grievances or fear. The administration hopes improved security and economic opportunities will persuade some of those fighters to lay down their weapons. Gates cautioned, however, that the Taliban’s senior leadership currently has little incentive to compromise.

## Reinforcements headed south

The 21,000-troop increase consists of approximately 17,000 combat and support personnel ordered to Afghanistan earlier in the year, along with roughly 4,000 additional troops assigned to train and advise Afghan security forces.

The first group includes:

- About 8,000 Marines, primarily for operations in Helmand province;
- An Army brigade of roughly 4,000 soldiers, intended to reinforce the south;
- Approximately 5,000 aviation, intelligence, engineering, medical and logistical personnel needed to support the expanded campaign.

The additional trainers will work with the Afghan army and police, which Washington considers critical to any eventual reduction in the international military presence.

The deployments are being conducted in phases, with most of the reinforcements expected to be in place during the summer fighting season. Moving the force requires more than transporting combat units: the Pentagon must also establish bases, expand airfields, deliver armored vehicles and helicopters, and build supply networks across Afghanistan’s difficult terrain.

The new forces will be concentrated largely in southern Afghanistan, particularly Helmand and Kandahar provinces, where the Taliban has maintained strong influence and where coalition forces have previously lacked enough personnel to hold territory after clearing it.

## Casualties expected to rise

Gates warned that the expanded campaign could lead to higher U.S. and coalition casualties. The expected increase does not necessarily mean the strategy is failing, officials said; it may instead reflect the fact that more troops will be operating in areas where the Taliban has long enjoyed freedom of movement.

Southern Afghanistan contains some of the insurgency’s most entrenched networks. Taliban fighters have built defensive positions, planted roadside bombs and established supply and taxation systems in rural districts. As American forces move into those areas, they are likely to encounter more ambushes, improvised explosive devices and direct attacks.

The increased troop presence will also produce more patrols and offensive operations, creating more opportunities for contact with insurgents. Operations are beginning as the warmer-weather fighting season accelerates, traditionally the period of greatest Taliban activity.

Military commanders intend to use the reinforcements to clear contested districts, remain in them and protect the population rather than withdraw after short raids. That “clear, hold and build” approach requires troops to stay exposed for longer periods while Afghan authorities attempt to restore government services and local security.

Helmand is expected to be particularly dangerous. The province is a major center of opium production, which helps finance insurgent networks, and its canals, compounds and agricultural fields provide cover for fighters and make armored movement difficult. Taliban forces have also planted large numbers of roadside bombs along routes used by coalition patrols.

## Pressure before reconciliation

Gates’s assessment reflects the administration’s broader view that military force cannot by itself end the conflict, but that negotiations attempted from a position of weakness are unlikely to succeed.

The immediate objective is to deny the Taliban the perception that it can wait out the United States and its allies. If insurgent commanders begin losing territory, recruits and access to local revenue, officials believe some factions may become more willing to accept the Afghan Constitution, renounce violence and sever ties with al-Qaeda.

That strategy carries substantial risks. Higher military casualties could weaken public support for the war, while civilian deaths could drive Afghans toward the insurgency. Commanders are therefore emphasizing tighter rules for airstrikes and greater protection of civilians, even when those restrictions increase danger to coalition troops.

Gates said the coming months are likely to be difficult as the reinforcements enter Taliban-held areas. The administration is betting that short-term increases in combat and casualties will eventually improve security, strengthen Afghan forces and create the conditions under which at least part of the insurgency will conclude that negotiation is preferable to continued war.
